title.analysis: Authentic title "Your Friends Are Secretly Making You Poor (The Friendship Tax)" uses an accusatory second-person frame plus a coined label. The script delivers an evergreen social-spending essay with mostly illustrative arithmetic. WEAK against a cohort containing "Pavement Princess" (152K) and "Snowball Effect" (65K). The low like count relative to comments suggests a polarising premise, but this is association only; no CTR or experiment evidence.

script.stored_text_completeness: All 19670 canonical characters read sequentially in full in 1 bounded ranges; auto-generated untimed text; stored ending is complete ("broke enough to figure that out."); ASR artefacts ("destination of bachelor party", "artisal pourover", "giftgiving"); fillers ("Um", "Uh"); the "hermit who eats ramen alone" line is repeated; audio, timed delivery and editing unverified.
script.opening_words: You're sitting at dinner with your closest friends. The bill arrives and someone suggests splitting it evenly. You ordered the cheapest thing on the menu and had water. Your friend ordered three cocktails and appetizer, the lobster, and dessert. You do the mental math. Your meal was $28. Your share of the split bill is 73. You smile, nod, and hand over your card because saying something would make you look cheap. Congratulations. You just paid a $45 tax for
script.ending_words: make you feel poor for having boundaries. Keep the ones who suggest the walk in the park. Your bank account will recover and your stress levels will drop and you'll discover something surprising. You're actually happier spending time with people who don't require you to perform financial stability you don't have. Turns out connection doesn't have a price tag. It just took you getting broke enough to figure that out.
script.analysis: Full 19670 canonical characters read. A social-spending essay: split-bill hook ($45 friendship tax), intro, social obligations, bachelor party and wedding costs, wedding season, birthday dinners, lifestyle creep (boat, wine), group trips, invisibility of the cost, pain-of-paying dilution, friend-group splits, saying no and a script for it, gift economy, wedding costs, social proof, social media, an individual-conversation framework, monthly social budget, "freedom fund", wedding alternatives, free activities and a close. Mostly illustrative arithmetic that reproduces. Verified: guest spending per wedding is within $300-700. Unsupported: $4,000/year average social spending; 50% marriage survival overstated; 90/10 friend split invented. "Over $2,000" per friend holds only at the higher gift. The stored ending is complete.
